conclusion.justification: The report concludes that rigorous evidence does not support hypnosis for smoking cessation and that 'no' is a reasonable characterization of the evidence, while acknowledging some nuance and low-quality studies showing potential benefits. This aligns with a cautiously unfavorable position (leans_reject).
conclusion.label: leans_reject

report:
Based on the available evidence, your assessment is largely correct: rigorous, high-quality research does **not** clearly support hypnosis as an effective smoking cessation method—though the picture is nuanced.

**The strongest evidence comes from Cochrane systematic reviews**, considered the gold standard for evaluating medical interventions. The Cochrane Review on hypnotherapy for smoking cessation found **insufficient evidence** to determine whether hypnotherapy helps people quit smoking more effectively than other methods or no treatment at all, largely due to high risk of bias in the underlying studies (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20927723/, https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD004407.pub4/full).

A 2024 Frontiers review similarly concluded that hypnotherapy's efficacy as a tobacco cessation intervention "cannot be considered sufficiently proven due to significant methodological limitations in the studies available" (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1330362/full).

A broader meta-analytic overview also found that among six effects reported across five reviews (including three Cochrane reviews), only two were statistically significant, with effect sizes ranging widely (d = 0.12 to 0.84)—suggesting inconsistent and generally weak evidence (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1330238/full).

**However, some nuance exists.** Newer, broader systematic reviews (e.g., a 2025 review of 63 studies) report more positive findings, and some smaller studies suggest promising quit rates. Critics note these more favorable studies often have weaker methodology, smaller sample sizes, or lack biologically confirmed abstinence measures.

**Conclusion:** The most rigorous evidence (Cochrane reviews) does not support hypnosis as a proven, effective smoking cessation method compared to other approaches. While some studies suggest potential benefit, methodological limitations prevent firm conclusions, making "no" a reasonable characterization of the current evidence base.
